description: Catholicism, diplomacy, slavery, and Japan’s first Western-style ship. The San Juan Bautista (St. John the Baptist) was a historic 17th-century Japanese-built galleon commissioned by the daimyo Date Masamune in Miyagi Prefecture. Its mission was to carry an embassy to Mexico. After this journey, the ship docked in the Philippines in 1618, where it was sold to the Spanish. By 1619, the Spanish were using the ship to transport slaves to Jamaica from Africa. During this voyage, however, the ship was attacked by English pirates, who took the slaves and sank the San Juan Bautista. Those slaves the English took became the first slaves in Virginia. In 2013, a replica of the ship was built here, in Ishinomaki City. The ship and its museum shine a light on a part of Japanese history that is often forgotten. There used to be a full-scale ship here, but after years of storms and decay, the ship was replaced with a smaller replica.
title: Japan's First Western Style Ship: The San Juan Bautista

description: Tucked away in the historic city of Aizu-Wakamatsu, one can stumble upon one of the most unexpected historical artifacts in Japan: a stone monument on Mount Iimori that serves as a strange, enduring link between two vastly different cultures. Erected in 1928, this structure was a gift from Benito Mussolini’s Italian Fascist regime, sent to honor the memory of the Byakkotai, or White Tiger Corps. This group of teenage samurai famously committed ritual suicide in 1868 during the Boshin War, a tragic act of loyalty that became a powerful symbol of bushido. The monument itself is a striking sight, featuring an authentic Roman pillar salvaged from the ruins of Pompeii, topped by a bronze eagle that gazes out over the Japanese landscape. The Italian engravings etched into the stone are particularly jarring to the modern observer, as they explicitly claim that the sacrifice of these young warriors demonstrated the core tenets and virtues of Fascism. It is a haunting, surreal intersection of ideologies, standing silently on a mountainside as a testament to how the narratives of history are often repurposed to suit the political ambitions of those far removed from the original tragedy. Exploring such a site reminds travelers that even in the most serene corners of Tohoku, there are layers of complex, sometimes uncomfortable history waiting to be discovered.
title: Benito Mussolini’s Monument to the Byakkotai

description: This population, found nowhere else on the planet, is due to a three century old local superstition. Sometime before 1738, a Japanese rat snake (a common, non-venomous species) was born with an albino mutation. Normally a mutation like that dies out within a generation or two. But locals protected the original snakes, finding their ruby red eyes and snow white scales so otherworldly that the snakes came to be seen as messengers of Benzaiten, the goddess of water and fortune. Small shrines and snake halls sprung up across the city, and the snakes officially became a protected species in 1972. In 2012, the city finally built them a proper shrine.
